concept.name: Quantitative tightening
concept.definition: The reduction of a central bank's securities holdings - by letting maturing bonds roll off without full reinvestment or, more rarely, selling them - which drains reserve balances and tightens financial conditions. It is the reverse of quantitative easing.
concept.intuition: If QE steps on the gas by adding reserves and holding down long rates, QT gently lifts off, letting the balance sheet shrink so bond markets stand on their own.
concept.mechanics: The FOMC caps reinvestment of principal payments from its System Open Market Account portfolio, allowing Treasury and MBS holdings to decline passively up to monthly runoff caps. The Fed began balance-sheet normalization this way in October 2017 and ran a second, larger runoff starting in June 2022.
concept.failure_modes: Runoff interacts unpredictably with banks' demand for reserves - the September 2019 repo-market spike forced the Fed to stop runoff and add reserves - and passive QT is slow to reverse if easing is suddenly needed.
concept.misconceptions: QT is not the same as raising rates: it operates on the balance sheet rather than the policy rate, and it usually proceeds passively through runoff caps, not outright bond sales.
concept.example: In October 2017 the Fed began capping reinvestment at $6 billion of Treasuries and $4 billion of MBS per month, stepping up quarterly to $30 billion and $20 billion; the 2022 runoff began at $47.5 billion per month and doubled to $95 billion after three months.

citations.source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Open Market Operations
